beginner: Calendula, also called pot marigold, is an easy, cheerful flower for cool weather. It is not the same plant as the marigolds you may know (those are a different plant called Tagetes). Calendula handles light frost, blooms in the cool parts of the year, spring and fall, and right through winter in mild-winter areas, but it fades and stops flowering in hot summer weather. The gold and orange petals are edible and add color to food, and the flowers have long been used in skin creams and salves. Plant the seeds in cool weather, snip off faded blooms to get more, and it will often drop seed and come back on its own.
seasoned: Calendula (Calendula officinalis), commonly called pot marigold, is a cool-season, frost-tolerant annual in the Asteraceae family, native to the Mediterranean. Despite the name, it is not a true marigold (those are Tagetes); it is a separate genus grown for single to double daisy-form blooms in gold, orange, yellow, and apricot. It thrives in the cool shoulders of the year, blooming almost continuously from spring or fall sowings, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones, but it languishes and stops flowering once sustained summer heat above roughly 85°F sets in. Plants tolerate frost to about 25°F, self-seed readily, and rebloom well with deadheading. The petals are edible, lending a saffron-like color to food, and calendula has a long traditional use in skin salves.

beginner: Calendula is easygoing and grows in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Moderately fertile, well-drained soil is ideal. It handles poorer soil too, but soggy ground rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and add a little compost if your soil is thin.
seasoned: Calendula wants well-drained, moderately fertile loam but is highly adaptable to a wide range of soil textures, from sand to clay, provided drainage is adequate. The consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil, which rots roots and crowns, especially in the cool, damp conditions calendula otherwise favors. It is a light feeder, so very rich soil pushes soft foliage at the expense of bloom and invites disease.

beginner: Calendula is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and you usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Calendula performs best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerates a little outside that range. It is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry, so pH adjustment is rarely warranted; focus on drainage and moderate fertility instead.

beginner: Plant calendula in cool weather, not summer heat. Sow the seeds in early spring and again in late summer or fall (and through winter where winters are mild). They sprout in a week or two and flower in about 6 to 8 weeks. Go easy on fertilizer, snip off faded flowers to keep more coming, and know that hot summer weather will slow or stop the blooms. Let a few flowers go to seed and calendula often replants itself.
seasoned: Treat calendula like a cool-season crop, the way you would spinach or lettuce: direct-sow into cool soil near 60°F, in early spring and again in late summer or fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in about 6 to 8 weeks. Go light on nitrogen, deadhead or cut for the vase to sustain bloom, and expect it to fade once sustained heat above about 85°F arrives. Leave a few heads to drop seed and it returns on its own.

beginner: Calendula does not need much feeding. Mix a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the soil before planting and that is usually plenty. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you leaves instead of flowers and more pest and mildew trouble.
seasoned: Calendula is a light feeder and needs little supplemental fertilizer. A modest balanced dose worked into the soil at planting is usually enough. Excess nitrogen pushes soft, leafy growth that flowers poorly and is more prone to powdery mildew and aphids, so favor a balanced or slightly lower-nitrogen feed and skip routine feeding once established.

beginner: It is a good time to give your calendula a little feed if you want. It does not need much, so one light dose of a balanced fertilizer is plenty, and you can skip it if you already worked some compost into the soil.
seasoned: Time for an optional light feed. Calendula is a light feeder, so one modest dose of a balanced fertilizer supports steady bloom; skip it if you mixed compost into the bed at planting.

beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For calendula, pick a balanced one like 10-10-10 rather than a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting suits calendula better than a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed, which favors foliage over flowers.

beginner: A little goes a long way. One light feeding when you plant is usually enough. If you do feed again, use about half the amount the package suggests, and avoid high-nitrogen feeds.
seasoned: A single light application at planting is usually sufficient; if supplementing, use a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annual flowers. Avoid repeated high-nitrogen feeding, which favors foliage over bloom.

beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that cluster on new growth, buds, and the undersides of leaves, leaving sticky honeydew and curled leaves. Calendula is a known aphid magnet. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and the flowers also draw in ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
seasoned: Calendula is notably attractive to aphids and is sometimes grown as a deliberate trap or banker plant. Soft-bodied sap-feeders colonize tender growth and buds, secreting honeydew and occasionally vectoring viruses. Usually held in check by the beneficial predators the flowers recruit; hose off or treat with insecticidal soap if populations build.

beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going, then water regularly but do not keep it soggy. Calendula likes steady moisture in cool weather, but wet, mucky soil rots it. Water the soil, not the leaves.
seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water regularly but moderately; calendula prefers consistent moisture in cool weather but resents waterlogged soil, which rots roots and feeds disease. Water at the base and avoid wetting foliage to limit powdery mildew.

beginner: Calendula likes about one inch of water a week, counting rain. Water the soil deeply a couple of times a week rather than a little every day, and let the top of the soil dry a bit between waterings. It needs less in cool winter weather.
seasoned: Aim for roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied at the base; let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Needs are lower in the cool, short days of winter bloom and higher as plants size up in spring.

beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. A soaker hose or watering can at the base works best, because dry leaves resist mildew. If leaves do get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep foliage dry; overhead wetting in the cool, humid conditions calendula favors invites powdery mildew and crown rot. If you must use a sprinkler, water in the morning so leaves dry fast.

beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems or crowns signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet foliage also raises powdery-mildew and damping-off pressure.

beginner: Calendula that is too dry wilts in the warmth of the day, looks dull, and makes smaller flowers. It is thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form.
seasoned: Wilting in the warmth of the day, dulling leaf color, and smaller flowers at bud point indicate underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bloom; chronic drought hastens the heat-driven decline of the planting.

beginner: Calendula is a flower for the garden and the vase, not food to store like vegetables. To make cut flowers last, cut them in the morning and put them in clean water. The orange and gold petals are edible: pull them off the flower, skip the bitter green base, and sprinkle them fresh on food for color (a cheap stand-in for saffron), or dry them on a screen and keep them in a sealed jar for tea or homemade salve. Only eat flowers that have not been sprayed.
seasoned: Calendula is grown for bloom, a pollinator draw, an edible petal garnish, and traditional herbal use, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as for produce. For cut flowers, cut in the cool of the morning into clean water and expect several days of vase life. The ray petals are edible: pull them from the flower head, discard the bitter green base, and use fresh as a slightly bitter, saffron-like color for soups, rice, salads, and butters, or dry them on a screen out of direct sun and store airtight for tea, color, and salve-making. Use only unsprayed flowers.

beginner: Pick the type for your spot. Tall kinds like Pacific Beauty and Indian Prince give long stems good for cutting; short, early kinds like Bon Bon and Calypso are great for the front of a bed or in pots. If you want calendula for skin salves or tea, look for Resina, a type grown for that. All calendula have edible petals, and the simpler, more open flowers are best for bees. Most come true from seed you save yourself.
seasoned: Choose by height and purpose. Tall strains such as Pacific Beauty and Indian Prince give long, cuttable stems for the vase and the back of a bed; dwarf, early types such as Bon Bon and Calypso suit edging, the front of a border, and containers. For herbal and salve use, growers favor high-resin selections such as Resina (often grown as single or semi-double flowers that are easy to pick). Most calendula are open-pollinated and come reasonably true from saved seed, and all are edible-petaled; single and semi-double forms serve pollinators best.

beginner: Calendula is a classic, cheerful companion plant grown to help the rest of the garden. Unlike true marigolds (Tagetes), it is not a proven soil-nematode fighter, so do not expect that from it. What it does well is bring in bees and helpful insects like hoverflies and ladybugs, whose young eat aphids. Gardeners also plant it as a trap or decoy because aphids love it, drawing them off nearby crops, and it traditionally goes near vegetables for color and pollinators. There is no plant you must keep it away from; just give it sun and room, and remember it likes cool weather, so pair it with other cool-season crops.
seasoned: Calendula's companion value is pollinator and beneficial-insect support, not the nematode suppression documented for true marigolds (Tagetes); pot marigold is a separate genus and should not be assumed to share that effect. Its open, nectar-rich flowers draw bees, hoverflies, lacewings, and ladybugs whose larvae prey on aphids, so it earns its place as an insectary edge. Because aphids are strongly attracted to calendula, it is also used traditionally as a trap or banker plant to pull aphids off a main crop, a tactic with a plausible mechanism but limited formal trialing. As a cool-season annual it pairs naturally with other cool-season vegetables and flowers. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site for sun and airflow.

beginner: Calendula flowers for a long time and bring in bees and helpful bugs like ladybugs and hoverflies. Their young eat aphids, so a calendula edge or border helps the whole garden.
seasoned: Calendula's best-grounded companion function. Its open, long-blooming flowers recruit bees and aphid-predators (hoverflies, lacewings, ladybugs, parasitic wasps), supporting biological control nearby. Plant it as an insectary edge or interplant for predator support and color; this is a habitat benefit, not a documented pest-repellent effect.

beginner: Aphids love calendula, so some gardeners plant it near aphid-prone crops to lure the aphids onto the calendula instead. Watch the calendula and wash off or remove the aphids there.
seasoned: A traditional trap-crop pairing. Calendula is strongly attractive to aphids, so it is planted near aphid-prone crops as a decoy to concentrate aphids on the calendula, where they can be hosed off, removed, or left for predators. The mechanism (a preferred host pulling pests off the cash crop) is sound, but the protective effect is traditional practice, not formally trialed; monitor and manage the aphids on the trap so it does not become a reservoir.

beginner: Calendula grows in the same cool weather as lettuce, cabbage-family crops, and peas, so it makes an easy, colorful companion in the cool-season garden, adding flowers and pollinators without crowding them for food.
seasoned: A cool-season habitat pairing. Calendula occupies the same cool shoulders as lettuce, brassicas, and peas, adding pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat and color with low nutrient competition. The benefit is ecosystem support and aphid-predator recruitment; keep it to edges and ends of rows so it does not shade lower crops.

beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week before planting them out. Calendula handles light frost, so it can go out a couple of weeks before your last frost.
seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need about a week of hardening off, increasing outdoor exposure gradually, before transplanting. Because calendula is frost-tolerant to about 25°F, transplants can go out a couple of weeks before the last spring frost.

beginner: The easiest way is to sow calendula seeds straight into cool garden soil (about 60°F), a quarter to half an inch deep, and cover them well because the seeds need darkness to sprout. They come up in one to two weeks. For a head start, sow indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost and move the young plants outside. You can pinch the tops once to make plants bushier.
seasoned: Calendula direct-sows readily into cool soil (about 60°F) at 1/4 to 1/2 in depth; cover the seed, because light inhibits germination. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and is the simplest method in the cool shoulders. To gain time in short-season areas, start indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant; calendula resents heavy root disturbance, so use cells or pots and transplant while young. Pinch once when young for bushier plants.

seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following calendula immediately with other susceptible asters where powdery mildew or aster yellows built up; rotate the bed to an unrelated family for a season if disease was heavy, and clear infected debris at season end. beginner: Rotating calendula is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it helps. Plant it in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season. Calendula reseeds itself, so you will often get new plants popping up nearby on their own.
seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast cool-season ornamental annual than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but moving calendula to a fresh bed and clearing infected debris limits carryover of powdery mildew and aphid-vectored virus. Because it readily self-seeds, expect volunteers, and thin or relocate them to keep airflow.

beginner: Cover the seeds well, about a quarter to half an inch deep, because calendula needs darkness to sprout. In cool soil they come up in one to two weeks.
seasoned: Cover calendula seed about 1/4 to 1/2 in; light inhibits germination, so darkness and cool soil near 60°F are the triggers. Seedlings emerge in 1 to 2 weeks.

beginner: Plant calendula in cool weather, not summer heat. Sow in early spring and again in late summer or fall (and in winter where winters are mild). Hot soil keeps the seeds from sprouting well.
seasoned: Sow into cool soil, the way you would spinach: direct-sow in early spring and again in late summer or fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones. Calendula germinates poorly in hot soil.

beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, space them about 8 to 12 inches apart. Room for air to move helps prevent the white mildew.
seasoned: Thin or space seedlings to 8 to 12 in once they have a few true leaves; generous spacing for airflow is the main cultural defense against powdery mildew.

beginner: Watch young calendula for aphids and slugs in cool, damp weather; aphids really like calendula. Spray them off with water or use insecticidal soap.
seasoned: Scout young calendula for aphids and slugs in cool, damp weather; calendula is an aphid magnet. Hose off aphids or use insecticidal soap, and the beneficials the flowers draw will help later.

beginner: Pinch off the top once when the plant is young to make it bushier with more flowers. Go easy on fertilizer so you get flowers, not just leaves.
seasoned: Pinch the growing tip once on young plants to force branching and more flowering stems; keep nitrogen modest so plants flower rather than run to soft, mildew-prone foliage.

beginner: Keep calendula in sun with room around it and water the soil, not the leaves. Dry, airy plants are what keep the white mildew away, especially as it warms up.
seasoned: Maintain full sun and airflow and water at the base; dry, well-spaced foliage is what keeps powdery mildew in check, sharpest as the weather warms.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist when the first flower buds appear, but not soggy. Too dry means smaller flowers; too wet rots the plant.
seasoned: Keep moisture even as the first buds form; drought stress at bud point reduces flower size and count, but never let the soil stay wet, which rots crowns and feeds mildew.

beginner: As buds form, check for aphids on them and for white powdery mildew in warm, damp weather. Catching crowding and wet leaves early keeps both down.
seasoned: Scout for aphids on buds and for powdery mildew as warm, humid weather arrives; addressing crowding and overhead wetness early limits both.

beginner: Snip off faded flowers back to the next leaves (or cut fresh ones for a vase) to get more blooms through the cool weather. Leave a few at the end to drop seed for next time.
seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf, or cut for the vase, to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom through the cool season. Leave a few late heads to self-sow.

beginner: Pick petals from fully open flowers on a dry morning, using only unsprayed plants. Pull off the colorful petals and skip the bitter green base. Use them fresh on food for color, or dry them and keep in a jar for tea or homemade skin salve.
seasoned: Harvest petals on a dry morning from fully open, unsprayed flowers; pull the ray petals and discard the bitter green base. Use fresh as a saffron-like color, or dry on a screen out of sun and store airtight for tea, color, and traditional salve.

beginner: To save seeds, leave a few flowers on the plant until they dry and turn brown, then collect the curved seeds. Calendula usually grows true from saved seed and also reseeds itself.
seasoned: To save seed, leave some heads to dry fully to brown before collecting the curved seeds; most calendula are open-pollinated and come reasonably true, and the plant self-sows freely.

beginner: One calendula gives you lots of flowers over the cool season. Short types make many small blooms; tall types make fewer, bigger flowers on long stems good for cutting or for picking petals. Keep snipping faded flowers and more keep coming until it gets too hot or freezes hard.
seasoned: A single calendula blooms generously over the cool season, carrying a steady succession of 2 to 3 in daisy flowers; dwarf types make many smaller blooms for color and edging, while tall strains give fewer, longer-stemmed flowers for cutting and petal harvest. Deadheading or cutting sustains production until heat or hard frost ends it.

beginner: Calendula flowers the same season you plant it, about six to eight weeks after sowing. There is no waiting year, and it often drops seed and comes back on its own.
seasoned: Calendula blooms the first season from seed, roughly 6 to 8 weeks after sowing, so there is no establishment year; a cool-season sowing flowers through the cool months and self-sows for the next.

beginner: Calendula quit flowering when it got hot
seasoned: Plants stopped blooming and got leggy in summer heat

beginner: Calendula does not like heat. When summer warmed up, it stopped flowering and got tall and tired. That is just how this cool-season plant behaves.
seasoned: Calendula is a cool-season annual; sustained heat above about 85°F stops flowering and makes plants leggy and mildew-prone. This is normal, not a mistake.

beginner: Plant calendula in the cool parts of the year, spring and fall, and skip the hot months. In mild-winter areas, grow it right through winter.
seasoned: Grow calendula in the cool shoulders and mild winters; sow in early spring and again in fall, and treat summer as its off-season in hot regions.

beginner: Give plants more room and sun, water the soil instead of the leaves, and pick off bad leaves. Growing in cooler weather helps most.

seasoned: Damping-off and root or stem rot struck plants in cold, wet, poorly drained soil; calendula rots if kept saturated in cool weather.

beginner: Plant in soil that drains well, do not keep it soggy, and give plants room for air.
seasoned: Sow into well-drained soil, do not overwater, and ensure airflow; avoid sowing into cold waterlogged ground.

beginner: A hard freeze killed the plants
seasoned: Plants killed by a hard freeze

beginner: Calendula handles light frost but not a hard, deep freeze. A hard freeze ended the plants.
seasoned: Calendula tolerates light frost to about 25°F but a hard freeze below that damages or kills it; in cold zones the first hard freeze ends the season.

beginner: Tiny bugs and sticky leaves (aphids)

beginner: Aphids, which love calendula, covered the new growth and buds and left everything sticky.
seasoned: Aphids colonized the plant; calendula is strongly attractive to them, clustering on buds and new growth, leaving honeydew and sometimes vectoring virus.

beginner: Cover the seeds well so they are in the dark, plant in cool soil, and keep it damp until they sprout.

beginner: For flowers all through the cool season, sow a new small batch of seeds every 3 to 4 weeks in spring and again in late summer and fall (and through winter where winters are mild). Stop during the hot months: calendula does not do well sown into summer heat.
seasoned: Sow successively every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool windows, early spring and again late summer into fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones, to keep fresh, vigorous plants in bloom. beginner: Calendula is mostly for cool-season color, pollinators, and its edible petals. Cut flowers for a vase when fully open and the stem feels firm, in the morning into clean water. To eat the petals, pick fully open, unsprayed flowers on a dry morning, pull off the colorful petals, and skip the bitter green base. Snip off faded flowers through the season to keep more coming.
seasoned: Calendula is grown for garden color, pollinators, cutting, edible petals, and traditional herbal use. Cut blooms for the vase when flowers are fully open and the stem is firm, in the cool of the morning into clean water; expect several days of vase life. Harvest petals from fully open, unsprayed flowers on a dry morning, pulling the rays and discarding the bitter green base. Deadhead spent blooms through the cool season to sustain flowering.

beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly: cut the old bloom back to the next set of leaves and the plant makes more flowers instead of going to seed. Cutting flowers for a vase or picking petals does the same job. Leave a few flowers at the end of the season to drop seed, and calendula often comes back on its own. Pinch young plants once to make them bushier.
seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf through the cool season to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom; cutting for the vase or harvesting petals serves the same function. Calendula reblooms well with regular deadheading and slows when it is allowed to set seed, though it self-sows freely if you leave the last heads. Pinch young plants once to force branching and more flowering stems.

beginner: In the cold northern states, calendula grows in one main season from a spring planting and blooms from early summer until a hard freeze. It handles light frost, so you can sow it a couple of weeks before your last frost. seasoned: In the northern tier, calendula is a frost-tolerant cool-season annual grown from a spring sowing for bloom from early summer to the first hard freeze. It handles light frost to about 25°F, so it can be direct-sown a couple of weeks before the last frost or started indoors for an earlier start. The far-northern zones (3 to 5) have cool enough summers that calendula blooms steadily through the warm months; in the warmer, more humid zones 6 and 7 it can slow in midsummer heat and is also grown as a fall crop.
